opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the underappreciated dynamics. Right now we're used to a world where AI companies compete partly by shipping. You train a model, you put it out through an API or a chat product, you get revenue and user feedback, and that funds the next run. Access is the business model.

But if you get to a point where AI systems can meaningfully automate AI research itself, so the model is doing a lot of the work of making the next model, then the calculus can change pretty dramatically. The most valuable use of your best model might not be selling it to customers at all. It might be pointing it inward, running thousands of copies on your own research problems, because every week you shave off your development cycle compounds. In that world, the frontier capabilities could increasingly live inside the labs, and what the public gets access to might be a generation or two behind, or a deliberately throttled version.

That has a few implications I worry about. One is that the gap between what outsiders can see and what actually exists could grow a lot. Policymakers, researchers, even the companies' own boards might be calibrating to the public models while the internal frontier is moving much faster. A lot of our current oversight implicitly relies on deployment as a forcing function: things get noticed when they're out in the world. If deployment lags far behind, you lose some of that early warning.

Another is on competition itself. A feedback loop like that can be very winner-take-more. If one company gets a lead in automated research and that lead lets them improve faster, small differences early on could turn into large differences quickly. That could push toward more concentration, and it could also make races feel more existential to the participants, which is exactly when you'd expect people to cut corners on safety testing.

There's also a compute dimension. In an intelligence explosion, the bottleneck shifts heavily toward compute to run all those automated researchers, so whoever controls compute, whether that's the labs, the cloud providers, or governments, gains a lot of leverage. And you could imagine governments stepping in once it becomes clear how strategically important this is, which changes the picture again.

So my main takeaway is that we should try to build transparency mechanisms now that don't depend on public release: things like reporting requirements about internal capabilities, how much of R&D is being automated, and what safety evaluations are run before models are used internally at scale. Internal deployment is still deployment, and in a fast takeoff it might be the deployment that matters most.

r001.rationale: The response says an early lead in automated research could compound into a larger advantage, but does not explain the specified case of companies growing independently along the same super-exponential curve.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that companies growing at the same constant exponential rate retain fixed wealth or power ratios.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that I keep coming back to is that right now, the way the AI industry works is that you have a handful of frontier labs, and the gap between them is really small. Like, if OpenAI or Anthropic or Google DeepMind releases something, the others are usually within six months to a year of matching it, sometimes less. And then there's a longer tail of open-weight models that lag by maybe a year or two. So the structure of the market is pretty competitive, and that competition is a lot of why access is so broad. You can get a pretty good model through an API for cents per million tokens, and that's because nobody can afford to charge much more without losing customers to someone else.

What I think an intelligence explosion does is it potentially breaks that equilibrium. If you get to a point where AI systems are substantially automating AI research, so you have something like millions of automated researchers working around the clock, then the rate of progress inside a lab could go from, say, doubling capabilities every year or so to doubling every few months, or even faster. And the crucial thing is that the advantage compounds. If you're six months ahead when that process kicks off, then in the old regime that's a modest lead. In the new regime, six months of algorithmic progress might be the equivalent of several years of the old pace. So the lab that gets there first could pull away in a way that's really hard to catch up with, because your lead in capabilities feeds into your lead in research speed, which feeds into your lead in capabilities.

And I think the implications for access are kind of two-sided. On one hand, you'd expect the frontier lab to have strong incentives not to release its best models, or at least not to release them openly. Partly for commercial reasons, because the model is now the crown jewel and you don't want competitors distilling it. But also partly for safety and security reasons, because at that point the model is doing things like automating cyber offense or bioweapons research, and governments are going to get involved. I think it's quite likely that at that stage, the most capable systems are only used internally, or are only available to a small set of vetted customers and government actors. So the gap between what the public has access to and what exists at the frontier could widen dramatically, from something like a year today to multiple generations of capability.

On the other hand, the stuff that does get released would still be incredibly capable by today's standards. So from the perspective of an ordinary user, you might still see a flood of amazing new products. It's just that you'd be getting the crumbs, in some sense, relative to what's going on at the top.

The thing I worry about is the concentration. If one actor, or one small coalition, ends up with a decisive lead in a self-improving system, that's an enormous amount of economic and potentially military power concentrated in very few hands. And the normal checks, like competition, like the ability of customers to switch providers, or the ability of other labs to replicate your results, those start to fail. So I think a lot of the governance question is: can you preserve some version of a competitive, pluralistic landscape, or at least set up oversight mechanisms, before you hit the point where the dynamics become winner-take-all? Because after that point, I think it's much harder to intervene.

r001.rationale: The response says an early lead in an accelerating AI research process compounds: capability gains increase research speed, which increases capability further, making the leader increasingly difficult to catch.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that companies growing at the same constant exponential rate retain fixed ratios of wealth or power.

astra-6.text:
I think an intelligence explosion could make competition much more winner-take-all. Right now, if one company has a better model, another company can catch up by doing more research, spending more on compute, and hiring good people. But if the better model is itself doing a lot of the research that produces the next generation, then being ahead could help you pull further ahead. A relatively small lead could compound into a very large one.

That’s not inevitable. It depends on how much AI actually accelerates research, what other bottlenecks there are, and how easily competitors can reproduce advances. But it seems like a real possibility that you go from several companies with roughly comparable capabilities to one company with a decisive advantage.

And I wouldn’t assume that company would keep making its best models available in the way companies do today. Selling access makes sense when that’s your main way to make money. If you can instead use the model internally to develop new technologies, build businesses, or improve the model further, broad access might become less attractive. You also have reasons to worry about competitors using access to catch up, alongside legitimate safety concerns.

So I’d distinguish between AI being widely available and the most powerful AI being widely available. We could have very capable, inexpensive systems that lots of people use, while the systems driving the next round of progress are held very tightly by one company—or by a company working closely with a government.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a lead could compound because a stronger model accelerates research, but does not explain the specified case of companies growing independently along the same super-exponential curve.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not explain that companies growing at the same constant exponential rate retain fixed wealth or power ratios.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an intelligence explosion could make the competitive dynamics much more winner-take-all. Right now, if one company gets ahead, other companies can often catch up. But if being ahead means you can use your AI systems to do the research that produces the next generation of AI systems, then that lead could compound. A company that starts only a little ahead could end up very far ahead.

And that could change the incentives around access. Today, companies have a strong reason to sell access to their models: that’s how they make money. But if a model can help you develop much more powerful models, giving other people access could mean giving away the thing that sustains your advantage. You might instead keep your strongest systems internal, use them for research, and sell access to less capable versions.

I don’t think that outcome is inevitable. It depends on how fast this process goes and how much competitors can learn from one another. But I wouldn’t assume that the current pattern—several companies offering broadly comparable models that lots of people can access—will persist through an intelligence explosion.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an early lead could compound into a much larger lead, but does not explain the specified case of independently growing companies on the same super-exponential growth curve or their increasing relative advantage.
